analysis.one_liner: Exempts landscaping and groundskeeping guest workers from the annual H-2B visa cap.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Every year, the number of H-2B visas — temporary visas for non-farm seasonal workers — is capped. This bill would have carved landscaping and groundskeeping workers out of that cap entirely, so landscaping companies could hire as many foreign seasonal workers as they wanted without limit. To offset that, it would have taken away an existing carve-out that fish roe processing workers enjoy. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Landscaping and groundskeeping companies that rely on seasonal foreign labor. By removing these workers from the annual visa cap, the bill would guarantee them a labor supply no longer subject to yearly limits, which is especially valuable during peak seasons when caps have historically run out.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the numerical limit on H-2B visas so that any worker employed (or offered employment) as a landscaping or groundskeeping worker, as defined by Bureau of Labor Statistics code 37-3011, does not count against the annual cap.
It pays for that expansion by repealing the existing statutory exemption that allows fish roe processing workers to bypass the cap.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. landscaping and groundskeeping workers, who would face more competition for seasonal jobs and potential downward pressure on wages; and fish roe processors, who lose their cap exemption.

drawbacks.text: Lifting the cap for landscaping workers would expand the supply of temporary foreign labor in that occupation, which tends to hold down wages and reduce bargaining power for U.S. workers in the same seasonal jobs.
H-2B workers are tied to a single sponsoring employer, so while the bill increases their numbers, it does not change their limited ability to switch jobs or negotiate.
The bill would strip the fish roe processing exemption, taking away a flexibility that industry currently has under the cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted favor to one industry: it gives landscaping employers an uncapped guest-worker pipeline while shifting the cost to American workers in the same occupation through added job competition, and pays for it by taking a carve-out away from a different industry. It offers little benefit to the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2020 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Joyce of Ohio introduced the bill on May 14, 2020, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill received one cosponsor, a Republican, and no further action was ever taken on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. landscaping workers, who avoided added competition from an uncapped guest-worker program; landscaping employers lost the chance at guaranteed seasonal labor, and fish roe processors kept their existing exemption.

for.name: Rep. David P. Joyce
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to exempt landscaping and groundskeeping workers from the H-2B visa cap.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 14, 2020 and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; the bill never reached a vote, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have let these employers hire unlimited H-2B seasonal workers outside the annual visa cap, guaranteeing labor supply. The cost falls on U.S. workers in the same occupation, who would face more competition in seasonal jobs.
The bill repeals the industry's existing exemption from the H-2B cap, removing a flexibility it currently enjoys.
